lesson.title: Come and Take It: Texas Breaks from Mexico
lesson.summary: American settlers invited into Mexican Texas grew estranged from Mexico City over slavery and centralized rule, and their 1835 to 1836 revolt created an independent republic that would later fuel the drive for continental expansion.
lesson.body:
When Mexico won its independence from Spain in 1821, it inherited a vast, thinly populated northern province called Texas. To attract settlers who could develop the land and defend it from raids, Mexico continued a Spanish era policy of granting large tracts to empresarios, land agents who recruited colonists in exchange for bringing in families. Stephen F. Austin became the most successful of these empresarios, bringing hundreds of American families into Texas in the 1820s. These settlers were the human expression of the expansionist mood described in Manifest Destiny: land hungry, mostly Southern, and confident that American style settlement belonged on the continent.

The arrangement soured quickly. Mexico abolished slavery nationwide in 1829, threatening the cotton economy many Texan settlers were building with enslaved labor, though Texas received exemptions and evasions for a time. Mexico City also grew alarmed at how quickly Americans were outnumbering Tejanos in the province, and the Law of April 6, 1830 tried to restrict further American immigration and impose tariffs. Then in 1835 the Mexican general and president Antonio Lopez de Santa Anna abandoned the federalist Constitution of 1824 and moved to rule as a centralist, stripping states, including Texas, of their local authority.

Armed resistance began that October at the Battle of Gonzales, where Texan settlers refused to surrender a small cannon under the banner "Come and Take It." Delegates declared Texas independent on March 2, 1836. Santa Anna personally led an army north to crush the rebellion, and his siege of the Alamo mission in San Antonio, defended by fewer than two hundred men including William Travis, Jim Bowie, and Davy Crockett, ended in a final assault on March 6, 1836 that killed nearly every defender. Weeks later, on March 27, Mexican forces executed several hundred captured Texan soldiers at Goliad, a massacre that hardened Texan resolve rather than breaking it.

The war turned at the San Jacinto River on April 21, 1836. Sam Houston led a Texan force in a surprise afternoon attack, shouting "Remember the Alamo" and "Remember Goliad," and routed Santa Anna's army in less than twenty minutes of fighting. Santa Anna himself was captured the next day and forced to sign treaties recognizing Texan independence, though the Mexican congress never ratified them.

The Republic of Texas existed as an independent, internationally recognized nation for nearly a decade, with Houston as its first elected president. Texans wanted annexation to the United States almost immediately, but successive American presidents hesitated, wary of adding another slave state and provoking war with Mexico. That hesitation would not last forever, and when the United States finally annexed Texas in 1845, it set the stage for the much larger war with Mexico that followed.
